# Marginal eligibility: strict feasible mass, graph preservation, and vertices

Let `mu` be the full-dimensional mixed volume source on finitely many
positive fibers `K_z`, `z in P subset Z^n`, as in the fixed-mass John
graph note, with `n>=1` and `d>=1`. Fix `0<t<=M=mu(S)`. For any real base `j`, define

    D(j)=inf {sum_(z in H) w_z:
                    H a closed base halfspace containing j},
    w_z=|K_z|.

For integer `j in P`, let `T(j)` be the maximum mass of a dominated
source whose base mean is `j`, and let `M_t(j)` be its fixed-mass
moment body whenever feasible. The results below do not prove the
restricted John-center selector succeeds at nonvertex bases.

## 1. The eligible base region is compact and convex

The set `D_t={j:D(j)>=t}` is convex. Indeed a closed halfspace
containing a convex combination of two points contains at least one
of them, so a halfspace through a combination of eligible points has
mass at least `t`.

It is closed: if eligible `j_k` tend to `j`, enlarge any closed
halfspace containing `j` outward by `epsilon>0`; it then contains all
large enough `j_k`, so has mass at least `t`. Letting `epsilon`
decrease to zero preserves that inequality by continuity of a finite
measure from above. For `t>0`, separation also gives
`D_t subset conv(P)`, making the region compact.

The already proved inequality `T(j)>=D(j)` makes every eligible
integer base feasible at mass `t`. The strict concavity of the John
volume root from
`candidate e40a05fd5546debc` therefore
still applies when maximization is RESTRICTED to eligible integer
bases. An integer convex average of eligible indices stays eligible.
Consequently the restricted maximizing set has no nontrivial integer
convex representation, has at most `2^n` elements by parity, and its
John-center graph has singleton integer sections. The same statement
applies to singleton sections if all eligible John volumes are zero.

At `t=M/2^n`, the weighted lattice centerpoint theorem supplies an
eligible integer index. It lies in `P`, since positive fiber indices
are lattice convex. This uses only the weighted Doignon centerpoint
bound, not OC.

## 2. Nonvertex eligibility gives strict feasible mass

**Lemma.** For `j in P`, equality `T(j)=D(j)` holds if and only if
`j` is a vertex of `conv(P)`. At a vertex both quantities equal `w_j`.

**Proof.** A vertex is exposed among this finite set by a linear base
functional. Every nonnegative source with base mean that vertex is
supported on its one fiber; hence `T(j)=w_j`. A closed base halfspace
isolating it gives `D(j)<=w_j`, while every containing halfspace counts
that fiber, giving equality.

Conversely use the attained dual of the finite mass linear program:

    T(j)=min_a sum_z w_z(1+a.(z-j))_+.

Its attainment is the ordinary finite-dimensional linear-program
attainment: the primal is feasible and compact, and the displayed
finite polyhedral dual has a finite optimum. Let `a` attain it and
write `q_z=1+a.(z-j)`. For all `0<s<=1`, the level set `q_z>=s`
is a closed halfspace containing `j`, with mass at least `D(j)`.
The layer-cake inequality is therefore

    sum_z w_z(q_z)_+ >= D(j).

If equality holds, no `q_z>1` is possible, because its contribution
above level one would be positive. Also no `0<q_z<1` is possible:
crossing that level would strictly lower the level-set mass, so the
mass could not equal `D(j)` almost everywhere throughout `(0,1)`.
Thus every positive `q_z` equals one, and every other `q_z` is at
most zero. In particular `a.(z-j)<=0` for all `z`, and

    F={z in P:a.(z-j)=0},
    T(j)=sum_(z in F) w_z.

If `a=0`, take `F=P`; the following argument is unchanged.
Suppose `F` contains a point `z_0` distinct from `j`. Choose a base
linear functional `b` with `b.(z_0-j)<0`. A halfspace

    (K a+b).(z-j)>=0

contains `j`, omits `z_0`, and for sufficiently large finite `K`
omits every point outside `F`: their `a.(z-j)` are strictly negative,
and there are only finitely many indices. When `a=0`, there are no
points outside `F`. Its mass is therefore strictly less than
`sum_F w_z=T(j)`, contradicting `D(j)=T(j)`.
Hence `F={j}`, so the functional `a` exposes `j` as a vertex.
This proves the lemma.

It follows that an eligible nonvertex satisfies

    t<=D(j)<T(j).

Its moment body is full dimensional, and the strict-mass support-dual
theorem applies in every continuous direction: its support point is
represented by an attained actual cap of mass `t` and base centroid
`j`, unique up to source null sets. Thus the marginal restriction
removes the boundary-mass dual-attainment issue at every nonvertex.

At an eligible vertex, `t<=w_j`. If equality holds, `M_t(j)` is the
singleton ordinary centroid of that original fiber. If strict,
`M_t(j)` is a full-dimensional ordinary trimmed moment body of that
one fiber. There are no other eligible singleton cases.

## 3. Every feasible point over a vertex satisfies the target budget

For completeness, let `K subset R^d` be a full-dimensional convex
body and let `sigma<=1_K dx` have mass `t>0` and centroid `y`.
Then every closed halfspace `H` containing `y` satisfies

    |K intersect H|>=gamma_d t.                       (1)

To prove this, take its nonzero continuous normal `u` and move its
boundary inward to `u.x=u.y`. Choose a parallel upper cap
`A=K intersect {u.x>=b}` of volume exactly `t`. Existence follows
from continuity of the volume tail, with `t=|K|` allowing `A=K`.
The threshold-exchange inequality gives

    integral u.x d sigma <= integral_A u.x dx,

so `u.y<=u.g_A`. The original cap contains
`A intersect {u.x>=u.g_A}`, whose volume is at least `gamma_d t`
by ordinary Grunbaum for the positive-volume convex body `A`.
This proves (1), including every closed threshold.

If `j` is a vertex, every represented source of a point of `M_t(j)`
is confined to the one original fiber `K_j`. Therefore (1) applies
to EVERY such point, not only its John center. For an ambient cap,
its restriction to that fiber is either a continuous halfspace or
the whole fiber; in the latter case its mass is at least `w_j>=t`.
Thus every feasible point above an eligible vertex has original
unnormalized depth at least `gamma_d t`.

At the proposed mass `t=M/2^n`, this is precisely the OC budget for
the vertex branch. If all restricted maximizing sections are
singletons, this branch settles that selector automatically.

## 4. What remains in the restricted selector question

A possible failure of the restricted largest-John-section selector
must be at an eligible NONVERTEX with a positive-volume moment body
and `t<T(j)`. Its actual John contact sources all have mass `t`, base
centroid `j`, and the exact covariance and integer-tilt identities
recorded in the fixed-mass graph and John-source notes. Marginal
eligibility has not been shown to cancel those integer tilts or to
control all other ambient tilts through the John center.

The parity bound describes only the number and convex-position
geometry of restricted maximizing bases. It supplies no further
continuous cap-mass factor in the nonvertex branch. No conclusion
about that unresolved branch is assumed here.
